title: Recursion
overview: A recursive routine is a function or procedure defined in terms of itself: it calls itself with a simpler input until a base case gives an answer directly. For the exam you must name the base case and general case, write recursive code, trace it with a trace table showing the calls winding up and then unwinding, describe how a stack of frames makes this possible, say what the compiler must produce, and judge recursion against iteration.
syllabusPoints: Show awareness of what a compiler has to do to translate recursive programming code.

definitions.definition: A process in which a function or procedure calls itself.
A function or procedure that is defined in terms of itself.
The stopping condition: an explicit solution that is returned without another recursive call.
The part of the definition that calls the routine itself, changes the state of the parameter and moves it closer to the base case.
The memory used for one call: its return address and the values of its local variables and parameters.
The calls made before the base case is reached, each pushing a new stack frame onto the stack.
Once the base case is reached, each call finishes in turn, its frame is popped and control returns to the previous call (last in, first out).
An error when the call stack runs out of space, for example because the base case is never reached or the recursion is too deep.
Repeating statements with a loop (FOR, WHILE, REPEAT) instead of calling a routine again.

sections.title: Concept of recursion: base case and general case
content: A recursive routine is defined in terms of itself. The factorial function is the standard example: 0! = 1, and for n above 0, n! = n × (n − 1)!. The second line is the general case; the first stops the process.
bullets: Recursion is a process using a function or procedure that calls itself.
It must have a base case (stopping condition) that gives a result without calling the routine again.
It must have a general case that calls itself recursively, changes its state (the parameter) and moves towards the base case.
Rule 1: a base case. Rule 2: a general case that moves closer to the base case on every call. Rule 3: the base case is reached after a finite number of calls.
A recursive call with an argument that never moves towards the base case recurses forever, ending in stack overflow.
Factorial(-2) breaks rule 3: n goes -3, -4 ... and never equals 0, so it fails to terminate.

examples.label: Spotting the two cases
examples.content: Power(Base, Exponent): Exponent = 0 is the base case (return 1). Return Base * Power(Base, Exponent - 1) is the general case: it calls Power itself and Exponent falls by 1 each time, so it reaches 0.

sections.title: How recursion is expressed in a programming language
content: In code, recursion is a function or procedure whose body contains a call to its own name. An IF statement separates the base case from the general case. A recursive function usually returns a value built from the result of the call; a recursive procedure usually outputs or changes something then calls itself.
bullets: Structure: IF (base case condition) THEN return/stop ELSE call itself with a changed argument ENDIF.
Function: the call sits inside an expression, for example n * Factorial(n - 1), so a statement (the RETURN, or the multiplication) is still waiting when the call is made.
Procedure: CALL CountDownFrom(n - 1) inside the procedure body.
Iterative alternative: the same task by a loop (e.g. FOR i ← 1 TO n with Result ← Result * i), with no routine calling itself.
Iterative Factorial(0) with FOR i ← 1 TO 0 does no passes and returns 1; recursive Factorial(0) takes the base case and returns 1.

examples.label: Recursive factorial (pseudocode)
examples.content:
FUNCTION Factorial(n : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   IF n = 0 THEN
      RETURN 1                       // base case
   ELSE
      RETURN n * Factorial(n - 1)    // general case: calls itself
   ENDIF
ENDFUNCTION

examples.label: Factorial with a guarded input domain
Iterative factorial for comparison (pseudocode)
examples.content:
FUNCTION FactorialIter(n : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
   DECLARE Result : INTEGER
   DECLARE i : INTEGER
   Result ← 1
   FOR i ← 1 TO n
      Result ← Result * i
   NEXT i
   RETURN Result
ENDFUNCTION

examples.label: Recursive procedure: count down (pseudocode)
examples.content:
PROCEDURE CountDownFrom(n : INTEGER)
   OUTPUT n
   IF n > 0 THEN
      CALL CountDownFrom(n - 1)
   ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

sections.title: Tracing a recursive subroutine
content: Trace one row per call, in call order. Statements placed after the recursive call cannot run until the deeper calls finish, so you show the unwinding as extra rows below the base case and write each output or return value on the row where it happens. Do not go back up the table to fill in earlier rows.
bullets: Write a row for every call, giving the parameter value and the condition tested.
Base case row: the call that makes no further call (condition TRUE for n = 0).
Then add rows for the calls unwinding, in reverse order (last call finishes first).
Statement before the recursive call (OUTPUT n then CALL): output appears while winding, in call order.
Statement after the recursive call (CALL then OUTPUT n): output appears while unwinding, in reverse call order.
For a function, give the returned value on each unwinding row; the value passes back to the call that made it.

examples.label: CountDownFrom(2) and CountUpTo(2): where the OUTPUT sits
examples.content:
CountDownFrom(2), OUTPUT before the call:
Call | n | n > 0 | OUTPUT
1 CountDownFrom(2) | 2 | TRUE | 2
2 CountDownFrom(1) | 1 | TRUE | 1
3 CountDownFrom(0) | 0 | FALSE | 0   (base case)
Output: 2 1 0

CountUpTo(2), OUTPUT after the call (IF n > 0 THEN CALL CountUpTo(n - 1) ENDIF, then OUTPUT n):
Call | n | n > 0 | OUTPUT
1 CountUpTo(2) | 2 | TRUE | (waiting)
2 CountUpTo(1) | 1 | TRUE | (waiting)
3 CountUpTo(0) | 0 | FALSE | 0   (base case reached, unwinding starts)
(2) CountUpTo(1) resumes | | | 1
(1) CountUpTo(2) resumes | | | 2
Output: 0 1 2

examples.label: Trace of Power(3, 4) (returns Base * Power(Base, Exponent - 1))
examples.content:
Call | Base | Exponent | Exponent = 0 | Return value
1 Power(3,4) | 3 | 4 | FALSE | 3 * Power(3,3)
2 Power(3,3) | 3 | 3 | FALSE | 3 * Power(3,2)
3 Power(3,2) | 3 | 2 | FALSE | 3 * Power(3,1)
4 Power(3,1) | 3 | 1 | FALSE | 3 * Power(3,0)
5 Power(3,0) | 3 | 0 | TRUE | 1   (base case reached)
(4) Power(3,1) | | | | 3 * 1 = 3
(3) Power(3,2) | | | | 3 * 3 = 9
(2) Power(3,3) | | | | 3 * 9 = 27
(1) Power(3,4) | | | | 3 * 27 = 81
Result: 81 (3 to the power 4)

examples.label: Output after the call: denary to binary (pseudocode)
examples.content:
PROCEDURE ToBinary(n : INTEGER)
   IF n > 1 THEN
      CALL ToBinary(n DIV 2)
   ENDIF
   OUTPUT n MOD 2
ENDPROCEDURE

examples.label: Trace of CALL ToBinary(13)
examples.content:
Call | n | n > 1 | OUTPUT
1 ToBinary(13) | 13 | TRUE | (waiting)
2 ToBinary(6) | 6 | TRUE | (waiting)
3 ToBinary(3) | 3 | TRUE | (waiting)
4 ToBinary(1) | 1 | FALSE | 1   (1 MOD 2, base case)
(3) ToBinary(3) resumes | | | 1   (3 MOD 2)
(2) ToBinary(6) resumes | | | 0   (6 MOD 2)
(1) ToBinary(13) resumes | | | 1   (13 MOD 2)
Output 1101, which is 13 in binary. The purpose is to output a denary number in binary.

sections.title: Running a recursive subroutine: stacks and unwinding
content: A recursive routine can only run if the compiler generates object code that uses a stack. Every call needs its own return address and its own copy of the local variables, and the most recent call must finish first, which is exactly the last-in, first-out behaviour of a stack.
bullets: A stack is LIFO: each recursive call is pushed onto the stack and is popped when the function ends.
This enables backtracking/unwinding so results are returned in the required order (last call first).
Each call pushes a stack frame: the return address and the values of local variables (and parameters).
Winding: frames keep being pushed until the base case is reached.
Unwinding: after the base case, the top frame is popped, its local values are restored for the call below and the result is passed back.
The compiler must produce object code to push return addresses and local variable values onto a stack with each recursive call.
It must also produce code to pop the return address and local variable values off the stack after the base case is reached.
Number of frames = depth of recursion: CountDownFrom(100) makes 101 calls (n = 100 down to 0), so 101 frames are on the stack at once.
Memory use and processor time rise with every call; too many frames, or no base case, gives stack overflow.

examples.label: Program used for the stack trace (pseudocode)
examples.content:
010 FUNCTION SumTo(n : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
020    IF n = 0 THEN
030       RETURN 0
040    ELSE
050       RETURN n + SumTo(n - 1)
060    ENDIF
070 ENDFUNCTION
080 DECLARE Total : INTEGER
090 Total ← SumTo(3)
100 OUTPUT Total

examples.label: Stack contents during Total <- SumTo(3)  (bottom of stack on the left)
examples.content:
Event | Stack (return address, n)
Call 1 from line 090, n = 3 | [090,3]
Call 2 from line 050, n = 2 | [090,3] [050,2]
Call 3 from line 050, n = 1 | [090,3] [050,2] [050,1]
Call 4 from line 050, n = 0 (base case) | [090,3] [050,2] [050,1] [050,0]
Return 0: pop frame, back to line 050 | [090,3] [050,2] [050,1]  then 1 + 0 = 1
Return 1: pop frame, back to line 050 | [090,3] [050,2]  then 2 + 1 = 3
Return 3: pop frame, back to line 050 | [090,3]  then 3 + 3 = 6
Return 6: pop last frame, back to line 090 | empty; Total = 6
The base case is reached with 4 frames on the stack; they are removed in the reverse order of being added.

sections.title: When recursion is beneficial: comparison with iteration
content: Recursion is worth using when the problem is recursive by nature, because the code can mirror the definition. Otherwise a loop is usually cheaper.
bullets: Benefit: recursive solutions are often more elegant, shorter and easier to write when the problem is defined recursively (factorial, tree traversal, binary search).
Benefit: less program code than the iterative solution, with no loop counters to manage.
Drawback: each call uses stack memory and processor time to push and pop frames, so large inputs use much more memory than a loop.
Drawback: tracing and debugging is harder, and too deep a recursion (or a missing base case) gives stack overflow.
Iteration: uses a loop, needs no stack frames, so is generally faster and uses less memory.
Some optimising compilers convert a recursive subroutine into an iterative one when producing object code.
Recursion is also central to declarative programming, where repetition is written as recursive rules.
Fibonacci coded recursively recomputes the same values: Fibonacci(20) makes 21,891 calls, yet a loop needs 20 additions.

examples.label: Recursive Fibonacci counting its calls
examples.content:
calls = 0

def fib(n):
    global calls
    calls = calls + 1
    if n < 2:
        return n  # base case: fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)  # two recursive calls

print(fib(10), calls)  # 55 177

sections.title: Writing recursive algorithms
content: Exam questions ask you to write or complete a recursive routine, or a recursive version of a loop. Decide the stopping value first, then write the general case so the parameter moves towards it, and check the very first call terminates.
bullets: Step 1: the base case, with the value it returns (or the action it stops on).
Step 2: the general case: call itself with a changed (usually smaller) parameter, then combine the result.
Step 3: check every possible starting value reaches the base case (reject invalid input such as a negative n).
Binary search recursively: base cases are Low > High (return -1, not found) and item at Mid (return Mid); the general case searches the half that can hold the item.
Binary tree: recursion visits the left subtree, the node, then the right subtree (in-order); the base case is a null (empty) pointer.
Using a result without returning it (missing RETURN on the recursive call) loses the value on the way back.

examples.label: Recursive binary search
Recursive binary tree insert and in-order traversal
Trace of binary_search(data, 34, 0, 6)
examples.content:
Call | low | high | mid | items[mid] | Result
1 | 0 | 6 | 3 | 21 | 34 > 21, search (4, 6)
2 | 4 | 6 | 5 | 47 | 34 < 47, search (4, 4)
3 | 4 | 4 | 4 | 34 | found, return 4
Unwinding: calls 2 and 1 each return 4 unchanged. Final result: 4.

rows: Loop condition becomes false / count ends

analysisChains.title: Why a recursive routine needs a stack
steps: Each call has its own parameter values, local variables and return address
These must be kept while deeper calls run, because the earlier call is unfinished
The most recent call must finish first, which is last in, first out, i.e. a stack
So the compiler produces code that pushes a frame per call and pops it as each call returns
analysisChains.evaluation: The stack is what makes unwinding possible: without a frame per call, the earlier values and return addresses would be overwritten.

analysisChains.title: What happens when the base case is missing or unreachable
steps: The routine keeps calling itself with a parameter that never meets the stopping condition
Every call pushes another stack frame
A stack overflow error stops the program
analysisChains.evaluation: A base case must exist and every call must move towards it; Factorial(-2) fails because n never reaches 0.

analysisChains.title: Recursion or iteration for a given task?
steps: Recursion mirrors recursively defined problems, giving shorter code
Each call costs stack memory and processing time, and Fibonacci repeats the same calls
A loop uses constant memory and is generally faster
An optimising compiler may turn the recursion into a loop anyway
analysisChains.evaluation: Choose recursion for naturally recursive problems such as trees where clarity matters; choose iteration for simple counting or very deep repetition.

examTips: For 'what is recursion': 'a function/procedure that calls itself'. Do not just say 'a loop'.
Two features for 2 marks: a base case (stopping condition) and a general case that calls itself, changes the state and moves towards the base case.
Explain the stack in terms: LIFO, each call pushes a frame (return address and local variables), popped when the call ends so the values return in the correct order (unwinding).
For the compiler, state both directions: push return addresses and local variable values with each call, and pop them after the base case is reached.
Trace tables: one row per call, mark the base case, then add unwinding rows. Show the output or return value on the row where it happens.
Advantage and disadvantage: elegant/less code against more memory and processor time (stack frames), with a possible stack overflow.
commonMistakes: Writing a recursive case that does not move towards the base case, so the routine never stops.
Omitting the base case, or putting it after the recursive call.
Filling in the OUTPUT column of a trace table for the unwinding calls on the wrong rows, or going back up the table.
Saying recursion 'uses a queue' or 'uses a loop'; it uses a stack.
Forgetting RETURN on the recursive call, so the answer is lost.
Giving only 'push' for the compiler and forgetting the 'pop after the base case' point.
Saying recursion is always faster or better; it usually uses more memory and time than iteration.

quickRecall.question: What is recursion?
quickRecall.answer: A process using a function or procedure that calls itself.

quickRecall.question: What must every recursive routine have?
quickRecall.answer: A base case (stopping condition) and a general case that calls itself, changes its state and moves towards the base case.

quickRecall.question: What is stored in a stack frame?
quickRecall.answer: The return address and the values of the local variables (and parameters) for that call.

quickRecall.question: Why is a stack suitable for recursion?
quickRecall.answer: It is LIFO: each call is pushed and popped as the function ends, so unwinding returns results in the required order.

quickRecall.question: What must the compiler produce for recursive code?
quickRecall.answer: Object code that pushes return addresses and local variable values onto a stack with each call and pops them off after the base case is reached.

quickRecall.question: What is unwinding?
quickRecall.answer: After the base case returns, each earlier call finishes in reverse order, popping its frame and passing its result back.

quickRecall.question: One benefit and one drawback of recursion?
quickRecall.answer: Benefit: elegant, shorter code for recursive problems. Drawback: stack frames use lots of memory and processor time, and can overflow.

quickRecall.question: What happens with Factorial(-2)?
quickRecall.answer: n never reaches 0, so the base case is never reached: infinite recursion ending in stack overflow.

quickRecall.question: What is the output of CALL ToBinary(13)?
quickRecall.answer: 1101, because the MOD output happens while unwinding.
